title: GENIUS Act
official_title: An Act to provide for the regulation of payment stablecoins, and for other purposes.
summary: The GENIUS Act creates the first U.S. federal law governing stablecoins — digital tokens designed to hold a fixed value, typically pegged to the dollar. Only licensed entities (banks, federally approved nonbank issuers, or state-licensed issuers with under $10B outstanding) may issue stablecoins for U.S. customers. Issuers must back every stablecoin dollar-for-dollar with U.S. cash or short-term Treasury securities and publicly disclose their reserves every month.
brief: Creates a federal licensing and 1:1 reserve requirement for stablecoin issuers, bans unlicensed stablecoin issuance in the U.S., and classifies stablecoins as neither securities nor commodities.

top_lines.headline: Only Licensed Issuers May Issue Stablecoins
subs: Three years after enactment, it is unlawful for any unlicensed person to issue a payment stablecoin in the United States

Three permitted issuer categories: bank subsidiaries, federally approved nonbank issuers chartered by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, and state-licensed issuers with $10B or less outstanding
Violations carry penalties of up to $1M per violation and/or up to 5 years in prison

top_lines.headline: 1-to-1 Reserve Requirement
subs: Permitted issuers must maintain reserves of at least 100% of outstanding stablecoins (an at-least 1-to-1 basis) at all times
Eligible reserves: U.S. currency, deposits at insured banks, Treasury bills with maturity of 93 days or less, overnight repo agreements backed by Treasuries, and government money market funds

Reserves may not be rehypothecated (pledged as collateral) except for margin obligations, standard custodial services, and limited liquidity needs — liquidity repos must be centrally cleared or have prior regulator approval

top_lines.headline: Monthly Disclosure and Certification
subs: Issuers must publicly publish monthly reserve composition — total outstanding stablecoins, amounts by reserve type, average maturity, and custody location
The CEO and CFO must certify the accuracy of each monthly report; false certifications subject to the same criminal penalties as federal securities fraud
A registered public accounting firm must examine each month-end reserve report

top_lines.headline: Stablecoins Not Securities or Commodities
subs: Payment stablecoins issued by permitted issuers are explicitly excluded from the definition of 'security' under the Securities Act, Exchange Act, and related laws
Payment stablecoins are also excluded from the definition of 'commodity' under the Commodity Exchange Act
Permitted issuers are excluded from the definition of 'investment company' under the Investment Company Act of 1940

top_lines.headline: Stablecoin Holders Prioritized in Bankruptcy
subs: In any insolvency proceeding, stablecoin holders have first priority claim on required reserve assets ahead of all other creditors
Required reserves are excluded from the bankruptcy estate under 11 U.S.C. Sec. 541(b), but the automatic stay under section 362 still applies to those reserves
New Sec. 362(d)(5) directs courts to use best efforts to enter a final order beginning ratable distributions to stablecoin holders within 14 days of the required hearing where reserves are available

likelihoodReason: Signed into law on July 18, 2025, as Public Law 119-27. The bill passed the Senate in June 2025 with bipartisan support and the House on July 17, 2025.

items.main: Names the Act the “Guiding and Establishing National Innovation for U.S. Stablecoins Act” (the “GENIUS Act”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines key terms used throughout the Act, including “payment stablecoin,” “permitted payment stablecoin issuer” (subsidiary of an insured depository institution, Federal qualified issuer, or State qualified issuer), “digital asset service provider,” “Stablecoin Certification Review Committee,” and “foreign payment stablecoin issuer.”
items.detail: Definitions apply throughout (codified at 12 U.S.C. 5901). The Stablecoin Certification Review Committee is chaired by the Secretary of the Treasury with the Chairs of the Board and the FDIC (Corporation) as members; it acts by 2/3 vote unless otherwise specified.

sections.label: Section 3 — Issuance and Treatment of Payment Stablecoins

items.main: Prohibits any entity other than a permitted payment stablecoin issuer from issuing a stablecoin in the United States, with the prohibition taking effect three years after enactment.
items.detail: The three-year grace period allows existing issuers time to obtain a license or wind down operations. Digital asset service providers may not offer or sell stablecoins from unlicensed issuers to U.S. customers after the effective date. The Secretary of the Treasury may grant limited safe harbors by regulation for de minimis transaction volumes or in unusual and exigent circumstances with prior congressional notification. Peer-to-peer transfers between individuals and self-custodied wallet transactions are explicitly exempt.

items.main: Requires all permitted issuers to maintain 1:1 reserves using only U.S. currency, demand deposits at insured banks, Treasury bills with maturities of 93 days or less, overnight repo agreements backed by Treasuries, or government money market funds.
items.detail: Reserves may not be pledged or rehypothecated except in limited circumstances: satisfying margin obligations in permitted repo investments, standard custodial arrangements, or creating liquidity for expected redemptions using cleared or pre-approved repurchase agreements. Issuers must publish the composition of their reserves monthly on their website, including total outstanding stablecoins, amounts by reserve type, average tenor, and geographic custody location. The CEO and CFO must certify accuracy of each monthly report; false certifications carry criminal penalties equivalent to those for false SEC certifications under 18 U.S.C. 1350.

items.main: State-qualified issuers may only operate under state supervision when their total outstanding stablecoins are $10B or less; growth above $10B requires federal approval.
items.detail: State payment stablecoin regulators have primary supervisory and examination authority over state-qualified issuers, but the Federal Reserve may intervene in unusual and exigent circumstances after 48 hours' notice to the state regulator. The Federal Reserve's intervention authority includes issuing cease and desist directives limiting redemptions and affiliate transactions; these directives automatically lapse if the Board does not affirm, modify, or rescind within 10 days of the issuer's response.

sections.label: Section 5 — Approval Of Subsidiaries Of Insured Depository Institutions And Federal Qualified Payment Stablecoin Issuers

items.main: Requires each primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator to receive, review, and decide applications to issue payment stablecoins, establishing a licensing and supervision framework.
items.detail: A regulator must notify an applicant within 30 days whether the application is substantially complete and render a decision within 120 days. Denial is permitted only if activities would be unsafe or unsound under the listed factors; issuance on an open, public, or decentralized network is not a valid ground for denial.

sections.label: Section 6 — Supervision And Enforcement With Respect To Federal Qualified Payment Stablecoin Issuers And Subsidiaries Of Insured Depository Institutions

items.main: Subjects permitted issuers that are not State-qualified (or are below the $10B threshold) to supervision, reporting, and examination by the appropriate primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator.
items.detail: Examinations assess operations, financial condition, and risks to the issuer's safety and soundness and to U.S. financial stability. Regulators must use existing reports and avoid duplication where possible.

sections.label: Section 7 — State Qualified Payment Stablecoin Issuers

items.main: Gives State payment stablecoin regulators supervisory, examination, and enforcement authority over State-qualified issuers in their State, with the Board able to participate by memorandum of understanding.
items.detail: Under unusual and exigent circumstances the Board may, after not less than 48 hours' prior written notice to the State regulator, take an enforcement action against a State-qualified issuer or its institution-affiliated party.

items.main: Bars a digital asset service provider from offering or selling a foreign-issued payment stablecoin in the U.S. unless the foreign issuer has the technological capability to comply, and complies, with any lawful order; lets Treasury designate violators noncompliant.
items.detail: Treasury may designate a noncompliant foreign issuer within 30 days of identifying a violation, in coordination with relevant Federal agencies.

items.main: Directs Treasury to seek public comment (beginning 30 days after enactment, for 60 days) on innovative methods to detect illicit activity involving digital assets, then conduct research evaluated by FinCEN.
items.detail: Comment topics include application program interfaces, artificial intelligence, digital identity verification, and blockchain monitoring.

sections.label: Section 10 — Custody Of Payment Stablecoin Reserve And Collateral

items.main: Allows a person to provide custodial or safekeeping services for stablecoin reserves, stablecoin collateral, or issuance private keys only if subject to supervision by a primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator, another listed Federal financial regulator, or a State bank/credit union supervisor.
items.detail: Custodians must also comply with the requirements of subsection (b) unless holding the property under specified exceptions.

sections.label: Section 11 — Treatment Of Payment Stablecoin Issuers In Insolvency Proceedings

items.main: In any insolvency proceeding of a permitted issuer, gives stablecoin holders a priority claim on the required reserves — ratable among holders and ahead of the issuer and other claimants.
items.detail: Adds section 507(e) to title 11, United States Code (Bankruptcy Code), and overrides the title 11 definition of “claim” for stablecoin holders.

items.main: Directs the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators, in consultation with NIST and other standard-setters, to assess and, if necessary, prescribe standards promoting compatibility and interoperability among permitted issuers and with the broader digital finance ecosystem.
items.detail: Standards may be prescribed under section 553 of title 5, U.S. Code, consistent with the National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (Public Law 104-113).

items.main: Requires each primary Federal payment stablecoin regulator, the Secretary of the Treasury, and each State payment stablecoin regulator to promulgate implementing regulations within 1 year of enactment through notice-and-comment rulemaking.
items.detail: Each Federal banking agency must report to the Senate Banking and House Financial Services Committees within 180 days after the effective date describing the regulations promulgated.

items.main: Directs Treasury, with the Board, Comptroller, FDIC, SEC, and CFTC, to study non-payment stablecoins (including endogenously collateralized stablecoins) and report to Congress within 365 days of enactment.
items.detail: Defines “endogenously collateralized payment stablecoin” as a digital asset that relies solely on the value of another digital asset created or maintained by the same originator to maintain its fixed price.

items.main: Requires the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators, beginning 1 year after enactment and annually thereafter, to report to the Senate Banking and House Financial Services Committees and the Office of Financial Research on the status of the payment stablecoin industry.
items.detail: Reports cover trends in payment stablecoin activities, among other topics, and may include a classified annex.

items.main: Clarifies that the Act does not limit banks' and credit unions' authority to accept deposits, issue digital assets representing those deposits, use a distributed ledger, and provide custodial services; authorizes regulated entities to engage in the Act's stablecoin activities.
items.detail: Federal banking agencies, the NCUA, and the SEC may not require covered institutions to treat custodied digital assets they do not own as a balance-sheet liability, or to hold regulatory capital against custodied assets except as needed to mitigate operational risk.

sections.label: Section 17 — Amendments To Clarify That Payment Stablecoins Are Not Securities Or Commodities And Permitted Payment Stablecoin Issuers Are Not Investment Companies

items.main: Amends federal securities and commodities statutes to clarify that payment stablecoins are not securities or commodities and that permitted issuers are not investment companies.
items.detail: Includes an amendment to section 202(a)(18) of the Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (15 U.S.C. 80b-2(a)(18)), among other conforming changes.

sections.label: Section 18 — Exception For Foreign Payment Stablecoin Issuers And Reciprocity For Payment Stablecoins Issued In Overseas Jurisdictions

items.main: Exempts a foreign issuer from the section 3 prohibitions if Treasury determines its home regime is comparable to this Act (including section 4(a)), it registers with the Comptroller, and it holds sufficient U.S. reserves for U.S. customers.
items.detail: The foreign issuer must not be domiciled in a country subject to certain U.S. measures; reciprocal arrangements may modify the U.S.-reserve requirement.

sections.label: Section 19 — Disclosure Relating To Payment Stablecoins

items.main: Amends section 13104(a)(3) of title 5, U.S. Code, to add an exclusion for payment stablecoins issued by a permitted issuer aggregating $5,000 or less from the referenced financial disclosure requirement.
items.detail: Inserts “any payment stablecoins issued by a permitted payment stablecoin issuer aggregating $5,000 or less held” into the existing disclosure provision.

items.main: Sets the Act's effective date as the earlier of 18 months after enactment or 120 days after the primary Federal payment stablecoin regulators issue any final implementing regulations.
items.detail: Effective-date section — timing only; no substantive effect.

underreported.section: Section 19 — Disclosure Relating to Payment Stablecoins
underreported.summary: Amends federal financial disclosure law to require federal officials and employees to disclose payment stablecoin holdings only if the holdings aggregate more than $5,000, creating an exemption from the existing requirement to disclose deposits without a minimum threshold.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is to regulate stablecoin issuance. This provision separately modifies federal ethics disclosure requirements for government officials holding stablecoins, creating a de minimis reporting exemption that does not apply to ordinary bank deposits. The provision is not referenced in the bill's title or in the regulatory framework sections.

underreported.section: Section 7 — Federal Reserve Override Authority for State-Qualified Issuers
underreported.summary: Grants the Federal Reserve authority to issue enforceable cease and desist directives limiting redemptions and affiliate transactions of state-qualified stablecoin issuers in 'unusual and exigent circumstances,' after only 48 hours' notice to the state regulator.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill establishes a state regulatory pathway as an alternative to federal licensing for issuers under $10B. This provision allows federal override of state regulatory authority in circumstances defined by the Board through rulemaking, and includes authority to suspend redemptions — a power that, if exercised, would directly affect stablecoin holders' ability to redeem their tokens.

AFL-CIO, Legislative Alert, July 14, 2025. Dear Representative: On behalf of the AFL-CIO, I am writing to urge you to oppose two bills on crypto currency that may soon be up on the House floor for a vote this week.

gaps: The act permits reserves to include tokenized versions of permitted reserve assets, provided they comply with applicable law, but does not specify what regulatory standard applies to tokenized reserves or which regulator oversees them.

The effective date is the earlier of 18 months after enactment or 120 days after the primary Federal regulators issue final implementing regulations — meaning the act can take effect at the 18-month mark even if those implementing regulations have not been finalized, with no provision addressing how it operates in that interim.

The act prohibits rehypothecation of reserves but permits exceptions for repo liquidity purposes with prior regulatory approval; the act does not specify the standard regulators must apply when granting or denying that approval.

The act covers payment stablecoins but does not address non-payment stablecoins (algorithmically collateralized or endogenously collateralized stablecoins) other than requiring Treasury to study them within one year.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Carter
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to voice my support for  S. 1582, the GENIUS Act of 2025, which will provide a clear regulatory framework for the issuance of stablecoins in the U.S. This bipartisan, industry-supported bill will finally give the stablecoin asset class clear rules of the road for the issuance and use of digital assets. The GENIUS Act will establish standards so that issuers are credible and stablecoins are quality assets in a rapidly innovating digital market. I encourage all of my colleagues to vote in support of the GENIUS Act.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Vindman
featured_quotes.text: as the vice ranking member of the Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development Subcommittee of the House Committee on Agriculture, I rise today in support of both the CLARITY and GENIUS Acts. These bills aren't perfect, but digital innovation is critical to our economy, and I support a regulatory framework that protects consumers in the financial system. However, I am concerned about the ability of certain officials to use these assets for self-enrichment at the highest levels of our government.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Meuser
featured_quotes.text: I also recognize President Trump's administration, crypto czar David Sacks, and SEC Chair Paul Atkins for  their efforts to reverse the Biden-era irrational opposition and misguided regulations that we lived with for 4 years toward innovation and now we are setting America back on a progrowth America First course. Mr. Speaker, the Senate's legislation built on 2 years of groundwork by the House, crafting a framework for stablecoins that protects consumers, the dollar, and unleashes private-sector innovation. This bill achieves three goals.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Gottheimer
featured_quotes.text: to not pass this legislation is deeply irresponsible. It will allow the Wild West to continue. This will protect consumers and ensure that the Trump coin and others are overseen, with protection and oversight from the CFTC. It is critically important for protecting consumers and protecting our country.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Haridopolos
featured_quotes.text: once again, we are showing that we can lead here in Washington, D.C., getting things done with the leadership of our President and our leadership here in the House, working together with the United States Senate. It shows that we are offering that certainty and stability once again for our economy to make America first. We are going to make the dollar dominant once again, and we are going to lead on digital currency payments.

added: Federal licensing requirement for all payment stablecoin issuers serving U.S. customers
1:1 reserve requirement backed exclusively by U.S. cash, short-term Treasuries, or equivalent
Monthly public reserve disclosure requirement with CEO/CFO certification
Criminal penalties of up to $1M per violation and up to 5 years imprisonment for unlicensed stablecoin issuance
First-priority bankruptcy claim for stablecoin holders on required reserve assets
Foreign stablecoin issuer registration and comparability determination process administered by Treasury
Federal Reserve override authority for state-qualified stablecoin issuers in exigent circumstances
Bank Secrecy Act anti-money laundering obligations extended to payment stablecoin issuers
modified: Securities Act, Exchange Act, Investment Advisers Act, Investment Company Act, and Commodity Exchange Act: payment stablecoins issued by permitted issuers removed from definitions of 'security' and 'commodity'
Bankruptcy Code Sections 362, 507, 541, 1109: payment stablecoin reserves excluded from estate; stablecoin holder claims given first priority; courts required to begin distributions within 14 days
Federal financial disclosure law: stablecoin holdings under $5,000 exempt from disclosure
removed: Requirement for banks providing payment stablecoin custody to record custodied assets as liabilities on balance sheets
Requirement to hold regulatory capital against stablecoin reserves held in custody beyond operational risk requirements

added: New Sec. 19 — amends STOCK Act financial disclosure (5 U.S.C. 13104(a)(3)) to exempt payment stablecoins aggregating $5,000 or less held
New Sec. 4(a)(11) flatly prohibits any permitted or foreign issuer from paying interest or yield (cash, tokens, or other consideration) on a payment stablecoin

New Sec. 4(a)(12) bars non-financial public companies from issuing stablecoins unless the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee unanimously votes they pose no material risk, plus consumer data-use/privacy limits
New defined term: "Stablecoin Certification Review Committee" (Treasury Secretary as Chair; Fed Chair and FDIC Chair as members; acts by 2/3 vote)
"USG" added to the U.S.-Government terms banned in a stablecoin's name; new exception lets pegged-currency abbreviations such as "USD" be used
Exigent-circumstance safe harbors now require Treasury to send Congress a justification (possibly classified) before issuing them
New Sec. 11(h) study by Federal regulators on stablecoin insolvency gaps, due 3 years after enactment
AML Sec 9 adds a report on whether stablecoin mixers/tumblers facilitate illicit activity and on the scope of "digital asset service provider"; report deadline cut to 180 days
Foreign-issuer eligibility adds a bar where the issuer's home country faces comprehensive U.S. sanctions or is a primary money-laundering-concern jurisdiction
modified: Insured-status section drops the carve-out that had let issuers disclose which reserves are backed by the U.S. full faith and credit

Foreign payment stablecoin issuer determination now allowed only upon a recommendation from each other member of the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee, with a justification published in the Federal Register
FinCEN guidance/rulemaking deadline extended from 2 years to 3 years
Insolvency priority (Sec 11) made ratable among stablecoin holders, and stablecoin reserves stay subject to the automatic stay (11 U.S.C. 362)
"Federal Trade Commission Jurisdiction" rule replaced with a broader "consumer financial law" preservation citing 12 U.S.C. 5515
Section 3 issuance rulemaking changed from discretionary ("may, as appropriate") to mandatory ("shall"), consistent with Sec. 13
State-chartered depository institution provisions rewritten around home-State liquidity/capital adequacy reassessed by the home-State supervisor, replacing the prior deposit-reserve requirement
removed: Deleted the annual-for-4-years recurring AML report cadence (replaced by a single report)
